scope: First school Maths mock: Year 1/AS Pure only
notes: Four original multi-step questions, not copied AQA questions. Proof applications and two-dimensional vector problems have worked mark-point answers.

questions.prompt: Let n be any integer. Prove by deduction that n³ − n is divisible by 6.
markPoints: These are three consecutive integers, so one is even.
One of the three consecutive integers is a multiple of 3.
The product has factors 2 and 3, so n³ − n is divisible by 6 for every integer n.
questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Year 1 Pure challenge
questions.modelAnswer: n³ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1). These are three consecutive integers, so one is even. One of the three consecutive integers is a multiple of 3. The product has factors 2 and 3, so n³ − n is divisible by 6 for every integer n.

questions.prompt: Prove that the square of any odd integer leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 8.
markPoints: Write the odd integer as n = 2k + 1 for integer k.
k and k + 1 are consecutive, so k(k + 1) is even.
Therefore n² = 8r + 1 for an integer r, so the remainder is 1.
questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Year 1 Pure challenge
questions.modelAnswer: Write the odd integer as n = 2k + 1 for integer k. n² = 4k(k + 1) + 1. k and k + 1 are consecutive, so k(k + 1) is even. Therefore n² = 8r + 1 for an integer r, so the remainder is 1.

questions.prompt: A, B and C have position vectors (−1, 2), (3, 10) and (k, 20). Given that A, B and C are distinct and collinear, find k and the ratio AB:BC.
markPoints: Collinearity requires AC to be a scalar multiple of AB, so (k + 1)/4 = 18/8.
questions.subject: Maths
questions.question: Year 1 Pure challenge
questions.modelAnswer: AB = (4, 8). AC = (k + 1, 18). Collinearity requires AC to be a scalar multiple of AB, so (k + 1)/4 = 18/8. k = 8. BC = (5, 10), giving AB:BC = 4:5.
